title: The Strategic Fiber of America: Kevlar’s Impact on Warfighters
gist: A CSET research fellow traces Kevlar from a 1965 DuPont lab accident to the material underpinning every U.S. servicemember's body armor, and flags two live signals: the Pentagon requested only $414 million for advanced materials in FY2025 — under a tenth of its trusted AI and autonomy request — and DuPont sold its Aramids division, including Kevlar and Nomex, to private-equity-owned Arclin in April for roughly $1.8 billion.

insights.claim: DuPont finalized the sale of its Aramids division — including both Kevlar and Nomex — to Arclin, a company owned by private equity firm TJC, in a deal worth roughly $1.8 billion.
insights.so_what: The material protecting every American servicemember's head and torso is now a PE portfolio asset — a concrete defense-industrial-base ownership change with pricing and capacity implications.
insights.quote: DuPont finalized the sale of its Aramids division this past April — which includes both Kevlar and Nomex — to Arclin, a company owned by private equity firm TJC, in a deal worth roughly $1.8 billion.
insights.speaker: Julie George

insights.claim: The divested Aramids division employed around 1,900 workers across five manufacturing facilities and generated $1.3 billion in net sales during 2024.
insights.so_what: Revenue and footprint figures let you size the asset: a ~$1.3bn-revenue business sold for ~$1.8bn, roughly 1.4x sales for a mission-critical defense input.
insights.quote: This division employed around 1,900 workers spread across five manufacturing facilities and brought in $1.3 billion in net sales during 2024.
insights.speaker: Julie George

insights.claim: Kevlar now joins Teflon and Lycra as products DuPont no longer manufactures, marking a pattern of a longstanding American industrial company exiting its signature materials franchises.
insights.so_what: A repeated divestiture pattern at DuPont is a signal about where the parent sees margin — and where strategic materials capacity is migrating to financial owners.
insights.quote: Kevlar now joins Teflon and Lycra as products DuPont no longer manufactures.
insights.speaker: Julie George

insights.claim: With the 2026 sale, aramid manufacturing operations now span the United States, Europe and Asia under the new ownership, making ownership structure and production geography inseparable parts of the supply chain equation.
insights.so_what: Geographic dispersion plus PE ownership of a sole-purpose defense input is exactly the supply-chain concentration risk that triggers DPA-style intervention or reshoring mandates.
insights.quote: making ownership structure and production geography inseparable parts of the supply chain equation
insights.locator: We should also consider the supply chain issues surrounding aramids
insights.speaker: Julie George

insights.claim: In Fiscal Year 2025 the Pentagon requested only $414 million for advanced materials, less than ten percent of what it requested for trusted AI and autonomy.
insights.so_what: A greater-than-10x funding gap between AI and the materials that physically enable hypersonics and stealth is a specific budget imbalance that could be corrected — watch for advanced-materials line items in future requests.
insights.quote: the Pentagon requested only $414 million for advanced materials — a figure that amounted to less than ten percent of what was requested for trusted AI and autonomy
insights.speaker: Julie George

insights.claim: Advanced materials is one of four emerging technology areas alongside biotechnology, quantum sciences and future-generation wireless that together total $752 million of the requested budget.
insights.so_what: Four emerging-tech categories splitting $752 million total quantifies how thinly non-AI emerging technology is funded in the defense budget.
insights.quote: together total $752 million of the requested budget
insights.speaker: Julie George

insights.claim: Advanced materials underpin hypersonics, directed energy and stealth capabilities, so underfunding them constrains three priority capability areas that remain on the United States' pared-down list of critical technologies.
insights.so_what: Materials are the hidden upstream constraint on the flagship programs — a bottleneck that may become visible as hypersonics programs hit production limits.
insights.quote: advanced materials underpin hypersonics, directed energy, and stealth capabilities and warrant more concerted attention
insights.speaker: Julie George

insights.claim: Robust investment in advanced materials could yield longer-range aircraft and missiles, enhanced protection for troops and vehicles, and improved platform agility — gains that compound across the force rather than accruing to a single program.
insights.so_what: Cross-platform leverage is the investment case for materials: the returns are diffuse, which is also why they are chronically underfunded.
insights.quote: Even with limited budgets, advanced materials are the backbone of several essential critical military technologies.
insights.speaker: Julie George

insights.claim: Advanced Functional Fabrics of America, a nonprofit Manufacturing USA Innovation Institute, and the Army's Small Business Innovation Research program are named as the concrete existing channels for early-stage materials work.
insights.so_what: Two named funding conduits are where early-stage materials startups can realistically access defense capital today.
insights.locator: Advanced Functional Fabrics of America is doing important work
insights.speaker: Julie George

insights.claim: Kevlar changed the Department of Defense's logic: instead of thinking of more steel as more protection, the United States went all in on lightweight, flexible, mobile, high-performance materials engineering.
insights.so_what: A doctrinal inflection from mass-based to materials-based protection — the same logic now driving drone-era survivability debates about weight and signature.
insights.quote: Instead of thinking of more steel as more protection, the United States went all in on lightweight, flexible, mobile, and high-performance materials engineering.
insights.speaker: Julie George

insights.claim: Kevlar is a para-aramid polymer fiber five times stronger than steel by weight, which is the physical property that made the protection-versus-mobility tradeoff solvable.
insights.so_what: The 5x strength-to-weight figure is the benchmark any next-generation armor material has to beat to justify displacement.
insights.quote: Kevlar is five times stronger than steel by weight
insights.speaker: Julie George

insights.claim: The Army pursued Kevlar in the 1970s after learning that a significant portion of Vietnam War combat casualties resulted from low-velocity fragments, not high-velocity rounds — a casualty-data finding that redirected materials investment.
insights.so_what: Casualty-mechanism data, not aspiration, drove the procurement shift — the reusable lesson being that protection investment should follow empirical wound distribution.
insights.quote: a significant portion of combat casualties were a result of low-velocity fragments during the Vietnam War
insights.locator: In the 1970s, the U.S. Army took a vested interest in Kevlar
insights.speaker: Julie George

insights.claim: There was an 18-year gap between Kevlar's 1965 discovery and its first battlefield use in the PASGT helmet and fragmentation vest worn by airborne units in Grenada during Operation Urgent Fury in 1983.
insights.so_what: An 18-year lab-to-battlefield lag is the realistic benchmark for materials transition timelines — a caution against near-term expectations from today's materials programs.
insights.quote: This was an 18-year gap between discovery and battlefield deployment.
insights.locator: The PASGT was worn by airborne units in Grenada
insights.speaker: Julie George

insights.claim: Kevlar was fielded in Interceptor Body Armor at the end of the 1990s with soft Kevlar panels stopping shrapnel and handgun rounds, and paved the way for composites in armored vehicle spall liners, helicopter crew protection, aircraft components and blast mitigation.
insights.so_what: The spillover from personal armor into vehicle and aircraft composites shows how one materials breakthrough propagates across platform categories.
insights.locator: Kevlar was also integrated into advanced body armor systems
insights.speaker: Julie George

insights.claim: Kevlar reached the battlefield only after commercial adoption in radial tires, industrial belts and cables, cut-resistant workwear, phone cables, fiber-optic reinforcement, police vests and NASA spacecraft — the commercial market funded the scale-up.
insights.so_what: Commercial-first scaling is the dual-use template: defense adoption followed a decade of civilian volume, which is how the cost curve got there.
insights.quote: Before the battlefield, Kevlar found its way into several useful commercial applications.
insights.speaker: Julie George

insights.claim: Kevlar-belted tires were later largely displaced by steel in the passenger market, yet this commercial setback did not weaken Kevlar's dual-use value across defense-related applications.
insights.so_what: A losing commercial application did not kill the material — evidence that materials platforms should be valued on their application portfolio, not their lead market.
insights.quote: this commercial setback did not weaken Kevlar’s dual-use value, especially across defense-related applications
insights.locator: While Kevlar-belted tires were later largely displaced by steel
insights.speaker: Julie George

insights.claim: Kevlar helped inspire or accelerate the broader aramid fiber ecosystem including Nomex, ultra-high-molecular-weight polyethylene fibers, fire-resistant industrial safety gear, smart textiles and wearable systems, and nanomaterials and graphene research.
insights.so_what: One material seeded five downstream categories — the spillover argument for why underfunding materials compounds over decades.
insights.locator: It has spun out (no pun intended) a series of advanced cutting-edge materials
insights.speaker: Julie George

insights.claim: Modern U.S. body armor now relies on a mix including Spectra and Dyneema, with Kevlar as one component in layered armor systems rather than the sole material.
insights.so_what: Kevlar's role has shifted from monopoly to component, which matters when assessing how defensible the acquired Aramids franchise actually is.
insights.quote: the U.S. military relies on a mix of advanced materials, such as Spectra and Dyneema, highlighting how Kevlar is one component in layered armor systems
insights.locator: Paving the Way for Advanced Materials on the Battlefield
insights.speaker: Julie George

insights.claim: Kevlar is a dual-use success that now touches drones, hypersonic systems, wearable soldier technologies, critical infrastructure and consumer technology, including undersea cables and aircraft parts.
insights.so_what: Undersea cables and drones give the acquired aramids business exposure to two fast-growing infrastructure categories beyond defense.
insights.quote: Kevlar is a dual-use success that now touches drones, hypersonic systems, wearable soldier technologies, critical infrastructure, and consumer technology.
insights.locator: Yet, Kevlar changed the United States Department of Defense's logic
insights.speaker: Julie George

insights.claim: DuPont built a multi-billion-dollar business around Kevlar supporting thousands of American jobs in production, R&D and distribution, which the author presents as the case for corporate-government research partnerships in dual-use innovation.
insights.so_what: The public-private returns argument is the political case for restoring advanced-materials funding — expect it deployed in budget advocacy.
insights.quote: With the creation of Kevlar, DuPont established a multi-billion-dollar business around the synthetic fiber
insights.speaker: Julie George
